prompt: What does the lesson say a design principle is?

choices.text: A law: code that breaks it is wrong
choices.why: Treating principles as laws is the misreading the section warns against; it ends in over-built code.

choices.text: A rule of thumb about where change will hurt
choices.why: Right. It is a question to ask when something is hard to change.

choices.text: A named solution with a known shape, such as an adapter
choices.why: That is a pattern; a principle is the reason a pattern has its shape.

choices.text: A checklist to run before writing a class
choices.why: Before anything exists there is no change to protect against, which is what a principle is for.

prompt: Match each SOLID principle to the question it asks.

pairs.right: who will ask for this code to change?
can a new case be added without editing working code?
can every child be used where its parent is expected?
does the policy depend on the detail, or the other way round?

prompt: What do all five SOLID principles have in common, according to the lesson?

choices.text: They were all written by Robert C. Martin around 2000
choices.why: Martin collected them; open/closed is Meyer's and substitution is Liskov's.

choices.text: They are all about dependencies
choices.why: Right. Lesson 2's fragile base class and class explosion were the same subject.

choices.text: They each require an interface for every class
choices.why: That is the over-built reading the section warns about.

prompt: In the single responsibility principle, what counts as a reason to change?

choices.text: Each method the class has
choices.why: A class with six methods owned by one actor has one responsibility.

choices.text: An actor: a person or group who asks for changes
choices.why: Right. Martin's later wording says a module is responsible to one actor.

choices.text: Each verb in the class's description, since a class should do one thing
choices.why: Doing one thing is advice for functions; split classes by verb and you get dozens of one-method classes.

choices.text: A bug report filed against the class
choices.why: Bugs are fixed wherever they are; the principle is about who requests changes in behaviour.

prompt: With the Sunday-skipping desk.py, a book lent on Monday 2 March 2026 comes back on Saturday 21 March. Two Sundays fall in between. How many cents is the fine?
hint: 19 calendar days, minus the Sundays, minus the 14 free days.

prompt: fine_days and calendar_days start out as identical functions. Why does the section keep both?

choices.text: Python cannot call one function from two methods of different classes
choices.why: It can; that sharing is exactly what desk.py did.

choices.text: Duplicated code is always better than shared code
choices.why: The section defends this particular duplication, not duplication in general.

choices.text: They answer to different actors
choices.why: Right. Alike by accident is not the same thing; sharing them let one team's change leak into the other's.

prompt: Match each piece of report.py to the actor who would ask for it to change.

pairs.right: the desk coordinator who reads it

prompt: Adding csv_report.py did not touch report.py. What does that guarantee?

choices.text: The fine rules and the mail code cannot have been broken by the change
choices.why: Right. A request from one actor reached only that actor's code.

choices.text: The CSV output is correct, since it reuses tested code
choices.why: The new class itself still needs checking; what is guaranteed is that the old code is unchanged.

choices.text: The report will now be sent through a real mail server
choices.why: ConsoleMailer still prints; replacing it is IT's change, not this one.

prompt: A colleague proposes splitting TextReport further, into one class per column and one for the total line. What does the section say?

choices.text: Do it: smaller classes are always closer to the principle
choices.why: Size is not the measure; the section warns against splitting by size.

choices.text: Don't: they would answer to the same coordinator
choices.why: Right. Code that changes together for one actor belongs together.

choices.text: Do it, but only in Java or Go, where each class needs its own file
choices.why: Files are not the point; the principle cares about which code changes together.

choices.text: Don't: the principle only applies to classes over a hundred lines long
choices.why: ReportService had under twenty lines and three actors; length is not the test.

prompt: by_kind.py printed child: None cents. Why None?

choices.text: The child membership charges nothing by law
choices.why: Nothing in the program says so; no rule for children existed at all.

choices.text: The chain had no branch for it, so the function ended
choices.why: Right. A Python function that reaches its last line returns None.

choices.text: days_late was 40, and Python returns None for numbers over 30
choices.why: The adult line in the same run handled 40 days without trouble.

prompt: How does Martin's statement of the open/closed principle differ from Meyer's of 1988?

choices.text: Martin forbids editing any file once it is committed
choices.why: Nobody means that; bugs are fixed by editing in either version.

choices.text: Meyer extends through an abstraction; Martin through subclasses
choices.why: It is the other way round: Meyer had inheritance in mind.

choices.text: Martin's opening is an abstraction; Meyer's was subclassing
choices.why: Right. The closed code then knows the protocol and never the new case's name.

choices.text: They are the same principle with a different name
choices.why: The name is the same; where the opening goes is what changed.

prompt: A function has one if/elif on the kind of member, and no other function asks that question. A new kind arrives. What does the section suggest?

choices.text: Add the elif for now; the axis has not shown itself yet
choices.why: Right. The opening goes in once the chain repeats or each new kind means a hunt.

choices.text: Introduce a protocol at once, since every if chain breaks the principle
choices.why: Opening code along every axis puts an indirection on every line; the section says to wait for the axis.

choices.text: Subclass the function's module for the new kind
choices.why: Modules are not subclassed, and inheritance as extension is the version lesson 2 measured.

prompt: Which files changed when the capped child rule was added? Choose every one that applies.

choices.text: capped.py, which is new
choices.why: Yes. The new rule lives there.

choices.text: main.py, the wiring
choices.why: Yes. Something has to say the new case exists: one import, one entry, one loan.

choices.text: charges.py
choices.why: No. It depends on the protocol and never learnt the new rule's name.

choices.text: policies.py
choices.why: No. Capped was written in its own file, importing only the protocol.

prompt: A child returns a book 15 days late under Capped(1000, PerDay(50)). What is the fine, in cents?
A loan arrives with the kind "staff", which has no entry in rules. What does charge_sheet do?

choices.text: Prints None cents, like by_kind.py
choices.why: That was the if chain falling off its end; a dictionary lookup does not fall through.

choices.text: Raises KeyError at the lookup
choices.why: Right. A missing rule fails loudly at the line that is wrong.

choices.text: Charges the adult rate, the first entry in the table
choices.why: Nothing in the function falls back to a default; it asks for exactly the kind it was given.

prompt: ReferenceBook.lend has the same name, argument and return type as Item.lend. Why does it still break the principle?

choices.text: Because it raises an exception, and a child must never raise one
choices.why: A child may raise what the parent's contract allows; this one refuses input the parent accepted.

choices.text: Callers rely on behaviour, and it refuses a day the parent accepts
choices.why: Right. A strengthened precondition; matching signatures do not make a substitute.

choices.text: Because Python checks behaviour at import time and finds a difference
choices.why: Python checks nothing; the failure appeared only when check_out called it.

prompt: Which change to a child of Item would still keep the substitution principle?

choices.text: lend refuses any date that falls on a Sunday
choices.why: That accepts less than the parent, a strengthened precondition.

choices.text: lend returns None when the item is out of stock
choices.why: That promises less than a later date, a weakened postcondition.

choices.text: The due date it returns is never a Sunday
choices.why: Right. Promising more than the parent is allowed; every caller's expectation still holds.

choices.text: lend changes the title of the item it lends
choices.why: Callers expect the title to stay put; that breaks an invariant they rely on.

prompt: A child may not strengthen the parent's preconditions, and it may not weaken the parent's ___ .
Square(3) handed to widen came out with height 10. Which promise did Square break?

choices.text: Its width and its height move independently of each other
choices.why: Right. To keep its own invariant the square had to break its parent's.

choices.text: A rectangle's area is always width times height
choices.why: 100 is 10 × 10; the area was computed correctly from the sides it had.

choices.text: A rectangle cannot be created with equal sides
choices.why: Nothing forbids that; Rectangle(3, 3) is fine.

prompt: Put the steps of writing a contract test for Item in order.
items: Write down what Item.lend accepts and promises
Turn the promise into an assertion against one object
Loop over every class that claims to be an Item, in a subTest
Add each new child's name to the tuple the day it is written
trap: The promise has to be stated before it can be tested; the children come after it, not before.

prompt: A MemberService registers members, prints their library cards and computes their reading statistics for the acquisitions team. Which principle does it strain, and how?

choices.text: Liskov substitution: a service cannot have three methods
choices.why: Substitution is about children and parents; there is no hierarchy here.

choices.text: Single responsibility: three different actors ask it for changes
choices.why: Right. Count the actors, not the methods: three actors, three reasons to change.

choices.text: Open/closed: registering a member edits the database
choices.why: Writing data is not modifying code; the principle is about editing source for a new case.

prompt: A team fixes a Liskov violation by adding if isinstance(item, ReferenceBook) to check_out. What does the lesson say about that fix?

choices.text: It is the standard repair, since the caller knows its own needs best
choices.why: The caller was correct; the lie is in the class that claims to be an Item.

choices.text: It is fine as long as a contract test also covers check_out
choices.why: A contract test covers the children, and would still fail for ReferenceBook.

choices.text: It treats the symptom and reopens the lending function for each new child
choices.why: Right. Every lending function needs the check, and each new refusing child needs another branch.

choices.text: It is needed because Python has no interfaces
choices.why: Java callers would need the same check; the problem is the hierarchy, in any language.

prompt: Same-day laptop loans turn out to be a permanent part of the library. What is the right response to the failing contract test?

choices.text: Delete Laptop from the tuple so that the contract test passes again
choices.why: That hides the violation; callers still trust a later due date.

choices.text: Change Item's promise to "not earlier", then reread every caller of lend
choices.why: Right. The parent's contract is a decision too; it may be weakened on purpose, never quietly by a child.

choices.text: Give Laptop a loan_days of 1 and let it come back a day late
choices.why: That makes the test pass by recording a due date that is false: laptops are due the same day.
